08-159.r: 'Planning and the Poor' → book by B.S. Minhas.

09-001.r: InvITs: dividend and interest income fully taxable at investor's slab (Statement-I wrong); InvITs recognised as borrowers under SARFAESI Act, 2002 (Statement-II correct).

09-002.r: Interest Coverage Ratio → how easily a firm pays interest on its debt; helps judge present and emerging lending risk; higher ICR is better.
09-002.t: Higher ICR means stronger debt-servicing ability; 'higher is worse' is the trap.

09-003.r: Insolvency → state of being unable to pay debts; bankruptcy → legal process (conclusion) liquidating assets; IBBI (1 October 2016) regulates under IBC, 2016.
09-003.t: Statements swap them: insolvency is the state, bankruptcy the legal outcome.

09-004.r: Inter-Creditor Agreement (Project Sashakt, Sunil Mehta Committee, 23 July 2018) → faster resolution of stressed assets of Rs. 50 crore+ under consortium lending; binding if 66% lenders agree.

09-005.r: S4A (Scheme for Sustainable Structuring of Stressed Assets) → RBI scheme, 13 June 2016, for deep restructuring of large corporate borrowers facing genuine difficulties.

09-006.r: RBI 'Storage of Payment System Data' (6 April 2018) → all payment data stored only in India; no public-sector ownership rule; audit report goes to RBI, not CAG.

09-007.r: Committee to boost cashless transactions → Neeraj Kumar Gupta Committee (April 2016); after demonetisation, Amitabh Kant committee on cashless economy.

09-008.r: Merchant Discount Rate (MDR) → fee a bank charges a merchant for accepting customers' card payments; compensates card issuer, PoS bank and gateways.

09-009.r: All ATMs linked by National Financial Switch (NFS) → built by RBI's IDRBT in 2004; taken over by NPCI in December 2009.

09-010.r: NPCI (set up with RBI's help) → promotes financial inclusion; launched RuPay, a domestic card payment system, in 2012. Both statements correct.

09-011.r: UPI (developed by NPCI) → instant inter-bank payments by mobile; likely result: mobile wallets not needed for online payments.

09-012.r: CBDC → payments possible without US dollar or SWIFT; can carry programmed conditions like a spending time-frame (China's digital yuan expiry).
hi: Central Bank Digital Currency (केंद्रीय बैंक डिजिटल मुद्रा)

09-013.r: Bitcoin (January 2009, Satoshi Nakamoto) → not tracked or issued by central banks; peer-to-peer between Bitcoin addresses; parties can stay anonymous.

09-014.r: NFTs → unique cryptographic tokens on blockchain; digitally represent physical assets; cannot be exchanged at equivalency, so not a medium of commercial transactions.
09-014.t: Fungible cryptocurrencies swap one-for-one; non-fungible tokens cannot.

09-015.r: Broad Money (M3) = currency with public + demand deposits with banks + other deposits with RBI + time deposits with banks.
09-015.h: M3 = M1 + time deposits with banks.

09-017.r: Withdrawing Rs. 1,00,000 cash → demand deposits fall and currency with public rises equally; aggregate money supply (M3) unchanged.

09-018.r: Liquidity, highest to lowest → currency, demand deposits, savings deposits, time deposits.
09-018.h: C-D-S-T: Cash, Demand, Savings, Time, from instant to locked.

09-019.r: Money multiplier rises with more banking habit (more deposits to lend); higher CRR or SLR lowers it; population rise need not raise it.
09-019.h: More deposits → bigger multiplier; higher reserve ratios → smaller.

09-020.r: Money multiplier in India = Broad Money (M3) ÷ Reserve Money (high-powered money, M0 or R).

09-021.r: Black money → illegal income, or legal income hidden from tax, on which income tax is not paid; curbs include Voluntary Disclosure of Income Scheme.

09-022.r: Main worry from black money → loss of revenue to the State Exchequer through tax evasion, cutting funds for welfare schemes.

09-023.r: Demonetisation (8 November 2016, Rs. 500 and Rs. 1000 notes) → aims: curb black money and fake notes, less cash, more digital, wider tax base; not GDP growth.

09-024.r: Paper Currency Act 1861 gave Government monopoly of note issue; first Government paper currency issued in 1862.
09-024.t: Earlier notes came from private and Presidency banks (e.g. Bank of Hindustan, 1770-1832).

09-025.r: Decimal coinage → 1 April 1957 ('Naya paisa'); 'Naya' dropped from 1 June 1964, becoming just 'paisa'.

09-027.r: Legal tender money → money a creditor is legally bound to accept in settlement of claims (banknotes; coins within set limits).

09-028.r: RBI can print notes up to Rs. 10,000 (Section 24, RBI Act 1934); Rs. 10,000 note issued 1938, demonetised 1946; reissued 1954, demonetised 1978.

09-029.r: Note issue → Minimum Reserve System (1956, amended 1957): gold plus foreign securities at least Rs. 200 crore, gold at least Rs. 115 crore.

09-031.r: RBI notes are backed by gold coin and bullion, rupee coin, Government of India securities and foreign securities (Section 33, RBI Act 1934).

09-032.r: Coins issued by Government of India (Ministry of Finance), circulated by RBI; four mints: Mumbai, Noida, Kolkata, Hyderabad.
09-032.t: Don't confuse: RBI issues notes; Ministry of Finance issues coins.

09-034.r: Currency expansion → more money supply, lower value of money, higher prices.

09-035.r: Demand-pull inflation causes → expansionary policies, fiscal stimulus, higher purchasing power; not inflation-indexed wages or rising interest rates.
09-035.h: Demand-pull: more money and demand chasing the same output.

09-036.r: Inflation → prices of goods rise and value of money falls; exchange rate does not improve (rupee also weakens).
09-036.h: Inflation is a seesaw: prices go up, money's value goes down.

09-037.r: Fall in inflation rate → prices rising more slowly than before; it does not mean prices have fallen.
09-037.t: Falling inflation is not falling prices; falling prices is deflation.

09-038.r: Inflation benefits debtors, producers, traders, farmers; hurts creditors, moneylenders, pensioners, fixed-income groups, savings account holders.

09-039.r: Inflation helps debtors (repay with cheaper money); creditors, fixed-interest bond investors, consumers and pensioners lose in real terms.
09-039.h: Inflation is the borrower's friend, the lender's enemy.

09-042.r: Zero inflation for a year needs the annual inflation rate to be zero in every week of the year (inflation measured week by week).

09-043.r: Inflation fell from 10.9% (1994-95) to 4.8% (1997-98): A true; foreign investment rose only slightly (4807 to 5353 million US $): R false.

09-044.r: Deflation → persistent fall in general price level of goods and services; opposite of inflation.
09-044.t: A fall in the rate of inflation is not deflation.

09-045.r: Base effect → impact of previous year's price level on current inflation rate; a low base shows a high rate.
09-045.h: Low base → high inflation rate; high base → low rate.

09-046.r: Double-digit inflation curbed by containing budgetary deficit and unproductive expenditure; revenue deficit fell from 3.3% of GDP (1990-91) to 2.5% (1992-93).

09-047.r: Stagflation → high inflation, slow growth, high unemployment; causes: spending-led inflation, falling industrial output, weak demand, currency appreciation hurting exports.

09-048.r: Bottleneck inflation → supply falls sharply while demand stays same, due to supply bottlenecks or inefficient distribution; tough for government (A, R true; R explains A).

09-049.r: Headline inflation → change in CPI for a typical household basket; core inflation → CPI change excluding volatile food and fuel. Both correct.
09-049.h: Core = headline minus the shaky items (food and fuel).

09-050.r: Core inflation = headline inflation excluding both food and fuel inflation; shows the long-run price trend.

09-051.r: Inflation now measured by CPI (Combined); WPI was main index till April 2014, so 'calculated on WPI' is now incorrect.

09-052.r: Inflation in India measured by CPI, WPI and Labour Cost of Living Index; RBI's key measure now CPI (Combined).

09-053.r: Headline inflation → CPI (Combined), base 2012 = 100; RBI adopted it as key measure in April 2014, replacing WPI.
09-053.t: Old answers say WPI; since April 2014 the answer is CPI-Combined.

09-056.r: At question time → inflation in India measured by Wholesale Price Index (WPI); later replaced by CPI (Combined).

09-057.r: Inflation target (4% CPI, ±2%, 5 August 2016 to 31 March 2021) set by Government of India with RBI, under RBI Act amended May 2016.
09-057.h: 4 ± 2: the band runs from 2 to 6 percent.

09-058.r: Annual inflation in 1991 (calendar year, monthly average WPI) → about 12.7%.

09-059.r: Food weight higher in CPI (45.9%) than WPI (24.4%); WPI excludes services, CPI includes them; RBI uses CPI (Combined), not WPI, since April 1, 2014.

09-060.r: CPI → covers goods and services; RBI uses CPI (Combined) for monetary policy; compiled by NSO and Labour Bureau, not Office of Economic Adviser.
09-060.t: Office of Economic Adviser (Commerce Ministry) compiles WPI, not CPI.

09-061.r: CPI-IW, CPI-AL, CPI-RL → Labour Bureau; CPI-UNME → CSO (discontinued April 2008); CPI-Urban, Rural, Combined → NSO.
09-061.c: Book gives no single answer: I, II and III are compiled by the Labour Bureau; only IV (CPI-UNME) was compiled by CSO (since discontinued), so (c) fits the old position.

09-063.r: CPI-IW base years → 1960 → 1982 (from 1988) → 2001 (from 2006) → 2016 (from September 2020); compiled by Labour Bureau.

09-065.r: Wage compensation (dearness allowance) of Central Government employees → Consumer Price Index for Industrial Workers (CPI-IW).

09-066.r: Dearness allowance of employees fixed using Consumer Price Index for Industrial Workers (CPI-IW).

09-067.r: WPI compiled by Office of Economic Adviser, Ministry of Commerce and Industry; current base year 2011-12.
09-067.h: Wholesale is trade, so WPI sits with the Commerce Ministry.

09-068.r: WPI base 1993-94 = 100 came in April 2000, not 1998; it cut primary articles' weight, raised electricity's. Base 2011-12: manufactured 64.23%, primary 22.62%, fuel 13.15%.

09-071.r: WPI with base 2004-05 → released 14 September 2010; base revised to 2011-12 on 12 May 2017 (effective April 2017).

09-074.r: WPI base years → 1981-82, then 1993-94 (question period), now 2011-12.

09-075.r: CCEA (19 October 2009) shifted WPI base from 1993-94 to 2004-05 with monthly release; new series from September 2010 (Abhijit Sen Committee).

09-076.r: WPI now released monthly only (all groups since February 2012; weekly release cut from October 2009); WPI gives less weight to food than CPI-IW.

09-077.r: Price index 330 (base 1960 = 100) → weighted mean of prices of selected items rose 3.3 times, not every item.

09-078.r: Producer Price Index → average change in prices producers receive; output PPI (goods leaving production) and input PPI (goods entering production).

09-079.r: Cost-push inflation → leftward shift (decrease) of aggregate supply curve, caused by rise in wages (A and R true, R explains A).
09-079.h: Cost-push: costs (wages) push prices up from the supply side.

09-080.r: Post-pandemic, central banks hiked interest rates to curb inflation, assuming monetary policy can counter rising prices (both true; II explains I); World Bank (2022) warned of recession.

09-081.r: Reducing interest rate is expansionary, not anti-inflation; inflation is controlled by raising interest rates, credit control, cutting money supply, controlling demand, rationing.
09-081.h: To cool prices, raise rates (contractionary policy).

09-082.r: Decreased money circulation (liquidity) helps control inflation; RBI uses monetary policy for this, so it is not only the Government's job.

09-083.r: Food inflation reasons → changed consumption patterns with rising incomes; structural constraints in food supply chain. Foodgrain area had not fallen steadily by 30%.

09-084.r: India's WPI inflation was negative only in mid-2009 (June–August) and rose sharply from October 2009 to February 2010; crude had fallen from 140 $ to 30 $ earlier.
09-084.c: Book's (a) is wrong: WPI inflation was negative only in mid-2009 and rose sharply from October 2009 to February 2010. A is false; R (crude's fall from 140 $ to 30 $) is true, so (d).

09-085.r: Oudh Commercial Bank (Faizabad, 1881) → first limited-liability bank with all-Indian board; Punjab National Bank (founded 1894, Lahore) → first Swadeshi bank.
09-085.t: Don't confuse: first Indian-managed limited bank → Oudh Commercial; first Swadeshi bank → PNB.

09-086.r: Financial inclusion steps → bank nationalisation, Regional Rural Banks, village adoption by bank branches (all three); also Lead Bank Scheme.

09-087.r: Earliest → Banking Regulation Act (10 March 1949); then First Plan (1951), SBI (July 1955), life insurance nationalised (1956), general insurance (1972).

09-088.r: Bank nationalisation → 14 major banks (assets above Rs. 50 crore) in July 1969; six more on 15 April 1980.

09-090.r: Chronology → first bank nationalisation (1969) → Regional Rural Banks (1975) → second nationalisation (1980) → NABARD (1982).

09-091.r: Nationalisation order → RBI (1949) → SBI (1955) → LIC (1956) → 14 major banks (1969).

09-093.r: Public sector banks excluding SBI Group → 20 at question time; after mergers (April 1, 2020), now 12 public sector banks including SBI.
09-093.c: Book gives no single answer: there were 20 public sector banks besides the SBI group when asked (option c); after the mergers there are 12 including SBI.

09-094.r: PSB amalgamation (announced August 2019; 10 banks into 4 from April 1, 2020; 12 PSBs left) → economies of scale, capital access, wider reach, global-size banks.

09-095.r: Capital infusion into PSBs (Rs. 1,18,724 crore, 2008-09 to 2016-17) did not rise steadily; five SBI Associate Banks and Bharatiya Mahila Bank merged into SBI (2017).

09-096.r: EASE Index (Enhanced Access and Service Excellence) → measures performance of public sector banks; not ease of doing business for MSMEs.

09-097.r: Commercial bank functions include buying and selling shares and securities for customers, and acting as executors and trustees of wills.

09-098.r: Public sector bank → Government holds at least 51% stake; e.g. Indian Overseas Bank, SBI, PNB; now 12 PSBs including SBI.

09-099.r: Bank of Punjab was a private bank; merged with Centurion Bank in 2005 to form Centurion Bank of Punjab.

09-100.r: ICICI Bank is private, not nationalised; ICICI formed 1955 (World Bank initiative) as development financial institution; ICICI Bank incorporated 1994.

09-101.r: ICICI Bank is not nationalised; Dena and Vijaya Banks merged into Bank of Baroda, Corporation Bank into Union Bank of India.

09-102.r: State Bank of India → 1 July 1955, by nationalising Imperial Bank of India (RBI took 60% stake).

09-103.r: Largest commercial bank in India → State Bank of India (HQ Mumbai; 22,406 branches, 65,627 ATMs/CRMs as on 31 March 2023).

09-105.r: Only Indian bank in global top 100 (S & P, April 2020) → SBI (55th); April 2024: SBI 47th, HDFC Bank new entrant at 74th.

09-106.r: SBI with NABARD formed 'Farmers Club' (Kishan club) in Uttar Pradesh to reach farmers and raise their bargaining power.

09-107.r: SBI Chairman from 7 April 2011 → Pratip Chaudhuri (till 30 September 2013); Dinesh Kumar Khara from October 2020; Challa Sreenivasulu Setty selected 29 June 2024.

09-108.r: PSB chairmen selected by Banks Board Bureau (from April 01, 2016), replaced by Financial Services Institutions Bureau (FSIB) from 1 July 2022.

09-110.r: 'Simply Click' credit card → SBI (15 September 2015) with seven e-commerce partners like Amazon India, BookMyShow, Ola Cabs.

09-111.r: First Indian bank to open a branch in China → State Bank of India (2006).
09-111.t: First Indian private bank branch in China → Axis Bank (Shanghai).

09-112.r: First Indian private bank branch in China → Axis Bank, Shanghai (January 2014), after Chinese regulator's nod in September 2013.

09-113.r: First moving ATM in India → ICICI (private bank), Mumbai, 12 December 2002.

09-114.r: 'e-Kisaan Dhan' app for farmers → HDFC Bank (June 2020): mandi prices, farming news, weather, seed information plus banking services.

09-115.r: New Bank of India merged with Punjab National Bank (1993); Oriental Bank of Commerce and United Bank of India merged into PNB from 1 April 2020.

09-116.r: Bank of Rajasthan merged with ICICI Bank on 13 August 2010.

09-117.r: Bank of Karad → closed after the securities scam; merged with Bank of India in 1994.

09-118.r: Long-term industrial finance → IFCI (July 1948), ICICI (January 1955), IDBI (July 1964): all three.

09-119.r: Bank types → Indian Bank: Public; ICICI Bank: Private; Citi Bank: Foreign; Saraswat Bank: Cooperative.

09-120.r: Foreign bank with most branches in India → Standard Chartered (UK, 100); HSBC 26, Deutsche 17, Citibank 14, BNP Paribas 5.

09-121.r: Bank origins → ABN Amro: Netherlands; Barclays: United Kingdom; Kookmin: South Korea.
09-121.t: ABN Amro is not from USA; Kookmin is not from Japan.

09-122.r: Chronology → SBI (1955) → Lead Bank Scheme (1969) → Regional Rural Banks (1975) → NABARD (1982).
09-122.h: S-L-R-N: SBI, Lead Bank, RRB, NABARD.

09-123.r: Private banks: FDI up to 49% from all sources via automatic route (February 2002, up from 20%); promoter minimum was 40%, not maximum 49%. Now FDI cap 74%.

09-124.r: Rural branches of all commercial banks including RRBs → about 37% (30 June 2012); about 36% at end-March 2023.

09-125.r: Lead Bank Scheme → RBI, December 1969, from Gadgil Study Group and Nariman Committee; a designated bank leads credit development in each district.

09-129.r: Service Area Approach (April 1989) → under Lead Bank Scheme; each rural or semi-urban branch served 15 to 25 villages.

09-130.r: District credit planning → done under the district's Lead Bank.

09-131.r: SIDBI → set up 2 April 1990 by Act of Parliament; HQ Lucknow; principal institution for financing and developing MSME (small industries).
09-131.h: SIDBI's head office is in Lucknow, UP.
hi: Small Industries Development Bank of India (भारतीय लघु उद्योग विकास बैंक)

09-136.r: Financial inclusion → banking for all, incl. zero or minimum balance accounts and financial services to low-income groups (all options).

09-137.r: Financial inclusion aims → services to the poor, growth of weaker sections, finance in rural areas, expanding banking infrastructure; shrinking it is not an aim.

09-138.r: Hindrances to financial inclusion → low income, illiteracy and lack of bank branches (all three).

09-139.r: Committee on Financial Inclusion → Dr. C. Rangarajan (constituted June 26, 2006; final report January 4, 2008).

09-141.r: Small Finance Banks (RBI guidelines November 2014) → savings vehicles; credit to small businesses, small and marginal farmers, micro and small industries; no young-entrepreneur aim.

09-142.r: Payments Banks → resident-owned mobile companies and supermarket chains can promote; can issue ATM/debit cards, not credit cards; cannot lend.
09-142.h: Payments Bank takes deposits but never lends.

09-143.r: Payments Banks recommended by Nachiket Mor Committee (formed 23 September 2013; report 7 January 2014) on financial services for small businesses and low-income households.

09-144.r: Shadow banking → bank-like lending by lightly regulated non-banking financial intermediaries; term coined by Paul McCulley (2007).

09-145.r: Bank → wide range of financial activities for many customers; NBFI (no full banking licence) → mainly term-loan needs of large companies.

09-146.r: NBFCs can acquire government securities (statement 1 false) but cannot accept demand deposits like savings accounts or issue cheques on themselves (statement 2 true).

09-147.r: Ombudsman Scheme for NBFCs, 2018 → from February 23, 2018 under Section 45 L, RBI Act 1934; free complaint redressal for NBFC customers.
